title: Let every spirit praise the Lord (Psalm 150)
hookLine: trumpets, harp, timbrel, cymbals, and everything that breathes

cards: Trumpet. Psaltery and harp. Timbrel and choir.
Strings and organs. High-sounding cymbals, then cymbals of joy. That's the last psalm in the book, and it reads like a finale: every player coming in at once, nobody holding anything back for later.

The book of Psalms carries joy and grief, anger and trust. It ends here, every instrument sounding, and then the music handed to anyone with breath in their lungs. Today's word is the one it's built on: Alleluia.

teach.b: First, the word. Alleluia is Hebrew, hallelu-Yah: hallelu, all of you, praise, and Yah, a short form of God's name. So it isn't a feeling, it's an invitation: everybody, praise God.
It came into Greek and Latin untranslated, and Catholics still sing it that way today. Second, the orchestra. Psalm 150 is six verses, and almost every line is a call to praise.
It moves out from the sanctuary to the sky, then through the band.
In the Douay-Rheims: "Praise him with sound of trumpet: praise him with psaltery and harp." Then timbrel and choir, strings and organs, and two kinds of cymbals. Nothing is held back.

Third, the last line. After all the instruments, it lands on the one everybody has: "Let every spirit praise the Lord. Alleluia." The Hebrew says everything that has breath; the Latin, and the Douay after it, say spirit.
You don't need a trumpet. You need lungs. Fourth, how Catholics keep this word.
The Alleluia is sung before the Gospel at Mass. Through the whole of Lent, the Church goes without it.

teach.h: SILENT IN LENT, BACK AT EASTER.
teach.b: On Easter night, at the Vigil, it comes back, sung three times, rising each time.

teach.h: LET EVERY SPIRIT PRAISE THE LORD.

teach.b: Over thirty-five days the path ran from the two ways of Psalm one, through the shepherd, the Miserere, the pilgrims' road, the depths and the rivers of exile, to a finale where everything that breathes is invited to join.

how: Catholics sing the Alleluia before the Gospel at Mass, omit it through Lent, and bring it back at the Easter Vigil; Psalm 150 is prayed at Morning Prayer in the Liturgy of the Hours.

o: a cry of mourning for the dead

games.q: you're writing the last line of the whole book of Psalms, after trumpets, harps and cymbals. what instrument do you finish with?
games.why: it ends with the one instrument everyone has: "Let every spirit praise the Lord. Alleluia."

practice: Notice your breath going in and out on its own, without you asking. On one long out-breath, let the word ride out quietly, al-le-lu-ia, then just breathe for a while, and do it again when you're ready.
If you pray, it's praise; if you don't, it's simply a long, slow breath out, noticing that you're alive.

wordCard.voice: Alleluia. From the Hebrew hallelu-Yah: all of you, praise God. The word the Psalms end on. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: all of you, praise Yah, a short form of God's name.

carryVoice: Your line: everything that breathes. Tomorrow, a gospel, read straight through. Day one hundred ninety-one, done.
